why: Neutral (third-person) wording of the fact-checker's notes for the catalogue, used by make_catalog.py in place of the research file's notes for these ids. Only pronouns and the verbs around them changed (for example 'I re-fetched the LROC page' -> 'the LROC page was re-fetched', 'by my calculation' -> 'by calculation'); no fact, number or source was added or removed. The research file keeps the original wording.

notes.artemis3-haworth: Verified: the PDF was downloaded live (identical MD5 to the earlier cached copy) and Table 1 was rendered from it; -86.75 / -23.67 is stated there. The live LROC page gives 336.3 E, which is -23.7 E. Caveat: the two sources are not independent. Henriksen's Table 1 centers equal the midpoints of the LROC mosaic lat/lon extents: (-87.39 + -86.11)/2 = -86.75 and (-34.98 + -12.36)/2 = -23.67. Both are LROC-team products. The two centers differ by 1.5 km. Haworth was in both the 2022 and 2024 lists, and NASA has not published a 2024 boundary. For context, the IAU Gazetteer center of Haworth crater is -87.45, -5.17 E.
notes.artemis3-malapert-massif: Verified: Table 1 and the Fig. 2 caption are in the live PDF, and the LROC page was re-fetched live. The table value is the midpoint of the LROC mosaic extents, so the two sources are not independent. The LROC center (-86.0, +0.3) is 1.3 km from the table value; the input said about 1 km. The region was in both the 2022 and 2024 lists. For context, the IAU center of Malapert crater is -85.00, 11.40 E, so the massif region lies poleward of it.
notes.artemis3-mons-mouton-plateau: Verified: the live LROC page was re-fetched; the center and bounds are as stated. The source is a single LROC product given to 0.1 deg. The mosaic credit also names Intuitive Machines, and its bounding box (about 88 km in latitude) is larger than the roughly 60 km plateau, so this is only a rough center. The bounding-box midpoint is -84.31, 31.05. IM-2 Athena (-84.7906, 29.1957) lies inside the mosaic bounds, about 15 km from this center. LROC says IM-2 was in the central portion of one Artemis 3 region but does not name it. This region is distinct from 'Mons Mouton'. For context, the IAU center of Mons Mouton is -84.60, 31.00 E.
notes.artemis3-mons-mouton: Verified: the pair order in Table 1 was rendered from the live PDF; the second pair is -85.43 / 31.83. The LROC product title was re-fetched live. Wikipedia independently confirms that Mons Mouton is the former 'Leibnitz Beta', which supports the 2022 Leibnitz Beta Plateau to 2024 Mons Mouton mapping, but NASA has not stated the rename. The coordinate is the 2022 region center. The point lies inside the LROC combined-mosaic bounds and about 25 km poleward of the IAU massif center (-84.60, 31.00), on the massif's southern part. IM-2 is about 20.5 km from this center. Medium because both the rename and the 2024 boundary are inferred.
notes.artemis3-nobile-rim-1: Verified: Table 1 was rendered from the live PDF and the pair order confirmed. The point lies inside the live LROC combined-mosaic bounds. Feature identity: the point is 39 km from Nobile's IAU center, about equal to the 39.6 km crater radius, and lies poleward and west of it. That fits Astronomy.com's 'southwestern rim'. Correction: the input cited NAC_ROI_MTMOUTONLOB, which is the 95-105 deg sub-solar sub-mosaic (B), not the combined mosaic, so it was replaced with LO1. This is the 2022 center; the region was retained in 2024.
notes.artemis3-de-gerlache-rim-2: Verified: the pair order was rendered from the live PDF. The point lies inside the live LROC combined-mosaic bounds; that mosaic's center, 293.3 E, is -66.7 E. Correction: the '31 mi' figure comes from Astronomy.com, not NASA. -88.22 is 54 km (33.5 mi) from the pole, which matches better than Rim 1's 40 km. It is also the closest of the nine 2024 regions; Haworth is next at 99 km, and Slater Plain lies beyond Slater crater at 58 km. The point is 23 km from de Gerlache's IAU center (-88.48, -88.34 E; radius 16.4 km), so the region spans the rim and outer flank. Medium because only one source gives the number and the pairing within the cell is inferred from order.
notes.artemis3-peak-near-cabeus-b: Verified: the live LROC RDR page was re-fetched on 2026-10-09; Center Lat -83.6 and Center Lon 291.2 are stated there. LROC's longitude domain is 0-360 east, so 291.2 converts to -68.8 E. The center encoded in the product names (P836S2912) agrees. The bounding-box midpoint is -83.64, -68.64. NASA published no numeric center, so this rests on a single LROC-team source given to 0.1 deg; medium is kept. Sanity check: -83.6 is 194 km (121 mi) from the pole, which fits Astronomy.com's 'about 125 miles'. The input attributed that figure to NASA, which was wrong; the NASA release gives no distances. For context, the IAU Gazetteer center of Cabeus B crater is -82.26, -54.58 E, so the region lies poleward and west of it. The region was new in Oct 2024.
notes.derosa2012-cr1-connecting-ridge: This is the center of an ESA Region of Interest (RoI), not a single illumination maximum. De Rosa calls CR1 one of the most promising areas. verified: Table 2 extracted from the arXiv PDF with pdftotext matches exactly. Stereographic X/Y recomputed from the lat/lon with R = 1737.4 km, X = k·sin(lon), Y = k·cos(lon) (lon 0 up, 90°E right); the result reproduces the table's X/Y. That confirms east-positive longitude and spherical, i.e. planetocentric, latitude. The equivalence CR1 = Mazarico Site 1 = Gläser 2018 C1 is confirmed in the Barker 2021 text.
notes.derosa2012-gr1-de-gerlache-rim: RoI center; longitude east-positive. A typo in the input's what_it_says is corrected (stray '-89.6952? no:'); the value is -88.6952. verified: Table 2 text extraction matches, and the X/Y recompute matches exactly. Barker 2021 confirms GR1 = Mazarico Site 11 (de Gerlache rim). It is 0.53 km from Bussey Point C.
notes.im-2-athena-landed: Verified: both LROC posts were fetched live. Wikipedia gives the same value but cites LROC, so it is not independent. The landed point is 158 km from the pole, matching LROC's 160 km for the target. It lies inside the LROC Mons Mouton Plateau mosaic bounds, about 15 km from that mosaic's center and about 20.5 km from the 'Mons Mouton' (Leibnitz Beta Plateau) center. LROC does not name the region that contains it. The lander lies on its side in a roughly 20 m crater.
notes.im-1-odysseus-landed: verified: LROC 1360, the NASA LRO news page, NASA NSSDC and the EGU25 abstract all give 80.13°S, 1.44°E (east), so no conversion was needed. Sanity check: the cached LOLA LDEM_80S_80M gives about 2593 m here, against 2579 m stated by LROC (14 m difference). The site is just poleward of 80°S. Press reports say it landed within about 1.5 km of the intended Malapert A site. No primary source giving a numeric target coordinate was found, so the target is left out.
notes.im-2-intended-target: verified: LROC 1401 was opened and states the coordinate verbatim (east longitude). A search for a second numeric source found only the NASA IM-2 press kit PDF (Feb 2025) and the DLR image page name only 'Mons Mouton', with no coordinates. LROC is therefore the only numeric source, though an authoritative one. Precision is 0.01° (about 300 m in latitude, about 30 m in longitude at this latitude). By calculation this point is about 0.37 km from the landed position, which is consistent with the reported '~250 m' given the rounding. This is a target point, not a landed position. Wikipedia says the target was originally a ridge near Shackleton and was moved to Mons Mouton before launch.
notes.change-7-planned-landing: verified: Wikipedia states the coordinate, but its only citation is a 2023 Weibo post (ref [4]). Its other landing-site reference, SpaceNews (Jan 2024), only says 'Shackleton'. The Planetary Society, Gunter's Space Page, a 2023 ThePaper interview with chief designer Wu Weiren ('several candidate sites identified') and a 2026 ITHome article ('south of 85°S') give no coordinates. The NSR payload paper (PMC10880881) could not be fetched because of a CAPTCHA; per the prior researcher and the Planetary Society it shows only a map. No official CNSA coordinate was found. The longitude is east. Sanity checks: the cached LOLA DEM shows this point (about 1632 m) within about 20 m of a local high (1647.5 m at -88.81, 123.71), which is consistent with a 'peak'. By calculation, using the IAU Shackleton center (-89.67, 129.78; D = 21 km), the point lies about 26 km from Shackleton's center, so roughly 15 km outside the rim rather than on it. Treat this as an approximate, unofficial candidate at 0.1° precision. Status: rolled out on Long March 5 Y14 on 19 Aug 2026; the launch was scrubbed about 23-24 Aug 2026 (Tropical Storm/Typhoon Narra and readiness) and delayed to 2027.
notes.lupex-chandrayaan-5-candidate: verified: opened the newsletter; the sentence 'could be 89.45°S, 222.85°E' is stated verbatim and attributed to a 2024 IAC talk by ISRO's P. Veeramuthuvel. Converted from 0-360 E: 222.85 - 360 = -137.15 (137.15°W). Independent corroboration of the region only: an ISRO SAC LPSC 2024 abstract studies the 'proposed LUPEX landing site' with an OHRC image centred at 89.2836°S, 140.556°W (= -140.556°E) on the same ridge, which by calculation is about 5 km away. Sanity check: the cached LOLA DEM shows the point (about 1954 m) is essentially at a local high (1957.5 m within 2 km), consistent with a ridge crest. The number is secondhand and hedged ('could be'), so it is a candidate and not a confirmed target. This is not a CLPS mission; launch is planned around 2028 or later on H3.
